semantic_correction.stem: After an uncomplicated diagnostic lumbar puncture, a client asks whether remaining flat for several hours is necessary solely to prevent a post-dural-puncture headache. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Yes. Remaining flat for several hours after lumbar puncture has a proven preventive benefit and should be used routinely even when the client feels well.
options.B: Yes. Longer bed rest is more protective than early mobilization, so the client should remain flat until the next scheduled assessment regardless of symptoms.
options.C: Yes. Ambulation after lumbar puncture increases the risk of post-dural-puncture headache, so activity should be delayed until the client is ready for discharge.
options.D: No. Routine prolonged bed rest is not supported solely to prevent post-dural-puncture headache; follow the prescribed postprocedure monitoring and activity plan.

semantic_correction.rationale: D is correct. A current multisociety practice guideline indexed in PubMed addresses prevention and management of post-dural-puncture headache after intentional or unintentional dural puncture. Randomized-trial evidence synthesized in Cochrane reviews and systematic reviews shows no preventive benefit from routine bed rest after lumbar puncture compared with earlier mobilization; in pooled analyses, bed rest did not reduce post-dural-puncture headache and may increase its occurrence. Therefore remaining flat for several hours should not be prescribed solely as prophylaxis after an uncomplicated diagnostic lumbar puncture. The client should instead follow the specific postprocedure monitoring and activity instructions appropriate to the procedure and clinical condition. A and B are incorrect because longer routine bed rest has not shown a prophylactic advantage. C is incorrect because available randomized evidence does not show that early mobilization increases post-dural-puncture headache risk.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Distinguish prophylaxis from customary postprocedure positioning: routine prolonged bed rest is not supported solely to prevent post-dural-puncture headache after lumbar puncture.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the correct-answer length cue, rebuilt all four prophylaxis statements to close length and specificity parity, freshly verified the 2024 multisociety PDPH guideline record and randomized systematic-review evidence, and limited the claim to the evidence-supported question of prophylactic bed rest.

audit_findings_append.source_authority: Multisociety PDPH guideline with Cochrane/PubMed systematic-review evidence
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — complications after procedures
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests evidence-based prophylaxis after diagnostic lumbar puncture with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. Randomized evidence does not support routine several-hour bed rest as effective prophylaxis against PDPH.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Longer bed rest has not demonstrated superior prevention compared with earlier mobilization.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Randomized evidence does not show that early mobilization increases PDPH risk after lumbar puncture.
option_audit.D: Correct. Routine prolonged bed rest is not supported solely for PDPH prevention; postprocedure activity should follow the client's prescribed clinical plan.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. D is the only response consistent with randomized evidence; A-C each incorrectly claim a prophylactic benefit from prolonged bed rest or harm from mobilization.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel post-lumbar-puncture teaching statements of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed.
